mcqs.question: A team's tests already catch most bugs before review. Why does review keep earning its cost anyway?
options: It spreads knowledge of the change and converts the approval into shared team ownership, not just the author's
It exists mainly to double-check that CI actually ran
It replaces the need for tests on low-risk changes
It is required for a compiler to accept the change
mcqs.explanation: Correctness overlaps with what tests catch, but knowledge-sharing and shared ownership are review's own value, unrelated to test coverage — a second person now understands the change and the team, not just the author, stands behind it. Review doesn't replace tests or gate on CI status by itself.

mcqs.question: A reviewer opens a PR and immediately leaves ten comments about variable naming before reading the logic. What's the risk in that ordering?
options: None — style should always be reviewed first since it's the fastest thing to check
Naming comments block merges longer than correctness comments do
Leading with readability can bury real correctness or design issues underneath a wall of style feedback
Style comments count against the author's performance review
mcqs.explanation: The checklist orders correctness and tests ahead of readability precisely because attention is limited — a reviewer who spends it on naming first is prone to rubber-stamping the logic underneath. Style should mostly be automated away rather than argued over in comments at all.

mcqs.question: A team spends a lot of PR-comment time debating import ordering and brace placement. What does that indicate?
options: The reviewers are unusually thorough and this is healthy
A tooling gap — a formatter and linter in CI should settle this before a human sees the diff
The codebase needs a full style guide rewrite before review can resume
Style disagreements are a sign the design itself is flawed
mcqs.explanation: Style is 100% consistent once a formatter/linter is configured, so arguing about it in review comments is wasted human attention that should go to correctness and design fit instead. It isn't evidence of thoroughness or a deeper design problem — it's a missing CI step.

mcqs.question: A reviewer blocks a PR saying "I would have structured this whole module differently," even though the approach was already agreed in a design doc. What's the issue?
options: The reviewer is exceeding review's scope by relitigating a decision that was already settled elsewhere
The comment is fine because any structural disagreement should block a merge
The reviewer should have raised this concern after merge instead
Design docs don't apply once code review starts
mcqs.explanation: Re-deriving an already-agreed design isn't a reviewer's job — that belongs to the design-review gate, and doing it as a merge-blocking surprise wastes the author's already-approved work. A pure taste preference, absent a correctness or maintainability reason, isn't grounds to block.

mcqs.question: A reviewer approves a large PR within thirty seconds of it appearing, having only read the title. What's the most reliable tell that this was a rubber stamp rather than a fast reviewer?
options: The PR was large, and large PRs always get rubber-stamped
The reviewer can't name anything specific they checked beyond CI being green
The author is senior, so review speed doesn't matter
The PR had no test changes
mcqs.explanation: The diagnostic is whether the reviewer can point to something concrete they actually evaluated — correctness, an edge case, a design question. "CI is green" alone means nothing was reviewed beyond what CI already checks. Speed alone isn't proof either way; some genuinely small diffs deserve a fast approval.

mcqs.question: A reviewer spends twenty minutes deeply tracing call sites for a one-line config value bump, then spends two minutes on a database migration touching a payment table. What's wrong with this allocation?
options: Nothing — every PR should get exactly the same depth of review for fairness
The migration should get less review since schema changes are usually low-risk
The depth is inverted relative to blast radius — high-risk changes like payment migrations warrant the deepest review, not low-risk config bumps
Config changes should never be reviewed at all
mcqs.explanation: Calibrating review depth to risk means spending the limited attention budget where the blast radius is largest — payment and migration code — not applying uniform depth regardless of stakes. Treating every PR identically isn't fairness, it's a fixed budget spent on the wrong line items.
